messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Vinh sat in the dim holding room for three weeks, learning quickly that survival depended on reading the men who guarded him. The trauma itself was defined by their overwhelming presence and sudden, unpredictable shifts in posture. When one of the guards would pivot or reach toward the door, Vinh’s chest would lock and a wave of nausea would rise so violently he had to press his palms against his thighs to keep from gasping. That first encounter with sudden male movements and physical distress planted the seeds for everything that followed. In the months after his release, the sudden appearances of other men and the rising nausea acted as direct cues, pulling the memory replay into the present moment the moment a stranger entered the room. The triggers actively fed the memory, keeping the film of captivity constantly active and unbidden. Each time the triggers of male presence and somatic pain surfaced, they directly summoned the memory, ensuring the past never stayed in the past. The memory replay did not stay confined to his mind; it actively summoned the trigger of male presence, turning ordinary encounters into sudden confrontations with the past. Because the triggers of male presence and sudden movement so reliably ignited that visceral alarm, Vinh began to construct rigid boundaries to keep the feelings at bay. He started avoiding any date or anniversary connected to the event, crossing them off his calendar with a cold dread, and he made it a nonnegotiable rule to always plan an escape route before entering a place. The triggers directly forced him into these maladaptive strategies, as the mere possibility of being cornered with a stranger became unbearable. Because the memory replay so reliably ignited that same visceral alarm, Vinh found himself compelled to adopt escape route planning and avoid anniversaries, with the unspooling film making the present feel unsafe and demanding immediate behavioral control. Over time, those careful plans and calendar avoidance did more than keep him safe; they actively altered how the past was stored. By deliberately detaching himself from the memories whenever they surfaced and refusing to mark the dates on which the captivity began, Vinh slowly starved the narrative of its context. The maladaptive strategies of avoidance and detachment gradually fractured the trauma memory, leaving him unable to explain clearly what happened or find the words to describe it, even though he knew exactly what had occurred. As the memory lost its structure, the fragmented replay did not stop; it simply migrated into his nervous system. The unexplainable, wordless film that played in his mind now bypassed his conscious thought and went straight to his threat appraisal, making his body believe the danger was still active. Memory directly fueled the threat system, so Vinh found himself feeling on guard even inside his own home, his muscles coiled tight against a danger that the memories insisted was near. The rigid escape route planning and calendar avoidance kept his nervous system hyper-vigilant, ensuring that every male presence remained a potent trigger rather than allowing habituation to occur, while the ongoing planned exits and memory detachment directly reinforced his baseline threat level, convincing him that the world remained an active containment zone. The maladaptive strategies thus directly sustained both his triggers and his pervasive threat state, locking him in a daily loop of calculation and dread. Now, at sixty-nine, Vinh still works as a plumber, a trade that requires him to crawl into tight utility rooms and work side-by-side with other men. Last Tuesday, while replacing a garbage disposal in a suburban kitchen, a senior technician leaned over his shoulder to check the under-sink pipes. Vinh’s neck seized with a sharp, familiar pain, and the wave of nausea returned instantly, flooding his mouth with the metallic taste of that old room. He pulled away, muttering that he needed more light, and quickly calculated the distance to the back door before the other man could speak. His wife noticed how his shoulders had hunched for months, how he flinched when delivery drivers approached the porch, and how he stopped attending neighborhood gatherings altogether. She finally insisted he speak to a clinician after he froze in his own driveway, certain that a neighbor’s sudden gesture to wave was actually a signal to capture him again. Vinh wants to stop living like a stranger in his own life. He hopes someone can help him find the words to tell his wife what he survived, so he can finally rest without watching the exits.
